abstract.p: Industrial decision systems repeatedly rank maintenance actions, production tasks, and resource requests using indicators that change as new observations arrive. Small fluctuations can repeatedly reorder near-equivalent alternatives, whereas excessive reliance on historical priorities can delay a necessary response. This study developed a Rolling Stability Index-based multicriteria decision-making (RSI-MCDM) framework that separates current preference evaluation from temporal control of the published ranking. The index measured displacement among alternatives shared by consecutive decision epochs. A conditional stabilizer combined current positions with historical positions anchored to the active set, and an exact sorting solution preserved a valid permutation without exhaustive optimization. An indicator-based alarm bypass retained the current evaluation during urgent conditions. The Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS), VIseKriterijumska Optimizacija I Kompromisno Resenje (VIKOR), an explicitly defined ELECTRE-inspired net-flow procedure, and Preference Ranking Organization Method for Enrichment Evaluations II (PROMETHEE II) were evaluated on identical synthetic streams with 5–20 alternatives and 4–8 criteria. Thirty paired random seeds were used for noise, abrupt-change, and withdrawal-and-return regimes, with additional computational checks up to 500 alternatives. In the 20-alternative noise regime, mean reversal counts decreased from 1,728.9 to 598.7 for TOPSIS and from 1,601.3 to 570.8 for PROMETHEE II, while top-choice disagreement with the noiseless reference decreased from 0.258 to 0.182 and from 0.228 to 0.152, respectively. At the reference threshold, frequent gate activation made the noise-regime results close to unconditional smoothing. Abrupt-change tests exposed the importance of the alarm bypass and the method-dependent cost of temporal inertia. The framework provides an auditable temporal control layer for industrial priority queues. Its evidence concerns reproducible simulation rather than plant deployment, and parameter selection must jointly consider stability, ranking fidelity, and response delay.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Multicriteria decision-making (MCDM) supports industrial decisions in which technical condition, production requirements, resource availability, and operational risk must be considered together. Maintenance teams use such evaluations to prioritize interventions; production planners use them to order competing tasks or resource requests. The Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS), VIseKriterijumska Optimizacija I Kompromisno Resenje (VIKOR), and outranking methods offer different ways to convert these criteria into a preference ordering. Their repeated use in connected production systems raises a further question: how should a priority queue change as new information arrives?

Connected production systems update equipment states, task requirements, and resource availability throughout an operating period. Alternatives enter or leave the candidate set, and observations of retained alternatives fluctuate. Each new evaluation consequently becomes part of a sequence of decisions. The resulting queue must respond to persistent changes while remaining usable for planning and preparation.

A persistent difficulty in this process is rank reversal. The relative ordering of existing alternatives may change when new alternatives are introduced, existing alternatives are removed, criterion values are modified, or the weighting structure is adjusted. Such changes are not necessarily incorrect, since genuine differences in alternative performance may justify a revised ranking. However, some reversals arise from the sensitivity of MCDM procedures to normalization, reference values, or the composition of the decision matrix rather than from substantial changes in the alternatives themselves. In streaming environments, repeated fluctuations of this kind may lead to unnecessary changes in operational priorities and reduce confidence in automated decision-support systems. Conversely, excessive restrictions on ranking changes may prevent a decision system from responding appropriately to changing operating conditions. Maintaining a reasonable balance between ranking stability and responsiveness is therefore an important requirement for dynamic industrial decision-making.

These difficulties are especially relevant at the interface between industrial analytics and operational action. A condition-monitoring model may produce a new health estimate at every acquisition interval, yet maintenance teams cannot rearrange an intervention queue at the same frequency without consequences for preparation and resource use. Similarly, a scheduling system may receive updated processing times and equipment states more frequently than operators can revise task assignments. A useful decision layer must therefore account for the persistence and significance of a ranking change, alongside the criterion values that caused it. The industrial contribution of such a layer lies in how it manages repeated decisions, rather than in replacing the underlying prognostic model or scheduling optimizer.

Rank reversal also has a narrower methodological meaning that must be separated from ordinary operational reprioritization. If an unchanged pair of assets exchanges relative order only because another alternative is added, the reversal can arise from the evaluation procedure. TOPSIS, for example, may change its normalized criterion values and ideal points when the comparison set changes. Analyses of TOPSIS and general decision models have established that this dependence deserves explicit scrutiny [1], [2], [3]. However, if one asset deteriorates or the decision maker changes the criterion weights, a new ordering can be justified. A temporal stabilizer cannot determine the validity of either change from rank positions alone. It can measure movement and control its persistence, but its outputs require evaluation against evidence that is independent of the smoothed ranking.

Recent research on industrial data streams examines how predictive models should adapt to changing process behaviour [4], [5]. That work addresses an upstream problem: whether the estimated indicators remain useful after the data-generating process changes. The present work addresses a downstream problem: how successive multicriteria outputs should become a priority queue. These problems interact but are not equivalent. A well-adapted predictor may still generate noisy priority changes, while an exceptionally smooth priority queue can conceal an obsolete predictor. The separation motivates independent logging of raw model outputs, raw MCDM rankings, and published rankings.

The research question is whether a transparent temporal control layer can reduce ranking oscillation across different MCDM methods while keeping the loss of current preference information visible. Three requirements follow. First, entry or withdrawal must not create artificial reversals among retained alternatives. Second, the stabilization rule must return a complete permutation, with an implementation that matches the mathematical objective. Third, the evaluation must assess the cost of stability through ranking displacement, agreement with a noiseless comparator, and recovery after an abrupt change. A decrease in reversal count alone cannot answer the research question.

The proposed Rolling Stability Index-based multicriteria decision-making framework, abbreviated RSI-MCDM, follows this separation. Baseline rankings supply a rolling measure of observed instability. The previous published ranking supplies a historical reference for conditional stabilization. Historical positions are embedded into the current active set before a squared-position objective is solved exactly by sorting. This construction avoids assigning invented past ranks to new alternatives. It also exposes the effective historical weight as a single parameter, preventing two mathematically redundant controls from being interpreted as independent sources of adaptation.

The contributions are fourfold. The first is a common-set rolling monitor with defined initialization, tie handling, valid comparisons, and attainable index bounds. The second is a separable, exactly solvable stabilization objective for changing alternative sets, accompanied by a proof and exhaustive small-instance checks. The third is an indicator-based alarm bypass that removes the continuity penalty during designated urgent conditions. The fourth is a paired simulation study of four ranking procedures, including unconditional-history and fixed-bound controls, alarm ablation, and a fully specified maintenance-queue interpretation. The evaluation quantifies when the rolling gate differs from continuous smoothing, including settings in which it offers little additional improvement.

The industrial setting is maintenance and production priority management, where alternative identities persist across repeated evaluations. The framework does not itself allocate crews, enforce machine-capacity constraints, or estimate failure probabilities. It produces a ranked input that can be passed to those downstream decision processes. The study evaluates controlled simulation, including an explicit maintenance-queue interpretation of the six-criterion configuration. The measured outcomes are ranking continuity, reference fidelity, and response delay.

Section 2 positions the method relative to normalization, dynamic decision analysis, and industrial intelligence. Section 3 specifies the rolling index, the exact stabilizer, and the ranking adapters. Section 4 describes the simulation protocol and metrics. Section 5 reports the numerical comparisons and sensitivity results. Section 6 discusses engineering interpretation and limits, and Section 7 concludes.

sec.title: 2.1. Rank reversal and the evaluation procedure
sec.p: Rank reversal has received considerable attention in multi-criteria decision analysis because the introduction of new alternatives or changes in evaluation conditions may alter the relative positions of existing options. The mechanisms responsible for this behaviour depend on the structure of the MCDM method being used. In VIKOR, ranking outcomes are influenced by the compromise formulation, the determination of reference values, and the balance between group utility and individual regret. Changes in the available alternatives may therefore affect the quantities used to establish the final ordering. In ELimination Et Choix Traduisant la REalité (ELECTRE), rankings are derived from concordance and discordance relations, making the results sensitive to preference thresholds and the composition of the comparison set. TOPSIS, by contrast, evaluates alternatives according to their relative distances from positive and negative ideal solutions. Because these reference solutions and the normalized decision matrix may change when alternatives are added, the relative ordering of existing alternatives can also be affected.

Recent TOPSIS analysis has examined how distance metrics and normalization interact when the alternative set changes [6]. Cluster-based normalization offers another way to address heterogeneous criterion distributions [7]. These approaches intervene inside the evaluator. Their relevance to temporal ranking is direct: if instability originates in a poorly matched normalization scheme, smoothing the output should not substitute for correcting that scheme. Nevertheless, an evaluator with fixed reference bounds can still respond to noisy measurements, because a change in measured relative performance remains a change in its input. This distinction motivates a fixed-bound TOPSIS control in the experiment.

Rank preservation is also considered in aggregation models that change how performance values and criterion weights are combined. The ratio product model explicitly addresses normalization and rank preservation [8]. Comparisons using a common normalization procedure further show why differences between complete MCDM pipelines should not be attributed to their final scoring formula alone [9]. Such studies concern the structure of a single evaluation or a controlled modification of its alternatives. RSI-MCDM instead leaves the chosen evaluator visible and adds a temporal publication rule after it. It consequently cannot inherit the axiomatic guarantees of a rank-preserving aggregation model merely by reducing observed reversals.

Sensitivity analysis examines how alternative performance, weights, and reference values affect an MCDM result. It identifies rankings that persist across admissible changes and the conditions under which preferences switch [10]. Temporal evaluation adds the duration and recurrence of those switches. A short-lived exchange between near-equivalent candidates can have a different planning consequence from a persistent change in the same pair.

Many rank-preservation analyses compare a baseline matrix with selected modifications. Streaming decision support requires a sequence-level view: the controller must account for how often a preference changes, how long the new order persists, and which alternatives remain comparable. These temporal properties motivate monitoring recent raw rankings before deciding whether to apply a continuity penalty.

Sensitivity analysis provides the natural link between these positions. The review by Więckowski and Sałabun [10] organizes ways of examining how MCDM results depend on input and modelling assumptions. Sensitivity and robustness are also treated as necessary safeguards against apparently precise but fragile decision outputs in social multicriteria evaluation [11]. The present experiments apply the same principle to temporal control parameters: a low reversal count is reported together with the displacement introduced by stabilization and the reference disagreement that remains. Parameter effects are therefore interpreted as trade-offs under a specified generator, rather than evidence of a universally optimal setting.

sec.title: 2.2. Dynamic preferences and temporal information
sec.p: Dynamic multicriteria analysis is broader than a time series of static score calculations. Criterion values, the available alternatives, the weights, and the decision context may all change. Dynamic three-way MCDM with uncertain linguistic information provides one example of ranking under changing evaluation information [12]. Multi-weight ranking addresses another dimension, namely how results depend on more than one admissible weighting description [13]. Criteria preprocessing and weight-based group decision reviews further emphasize that the criterion representation and preference structure are substantive parts of the decision problem [14], [15]. A temporal rule must therefore state which elements are held comparable across epochs.

In this study the criterion definitions and weights remain fixed within a run. Alternative membership and criterion observations change. This restriction allows ranking instability caused by measurement noise and membership changes to be distinguished from deliberate preference revision. A change in criterion meaning would break that comparison. For example, replacing a machine-vibration indicator with a remaining-useful-life estimate under the same column label would create a false impression of continuity. Such a change requires a new decision-model version and an explicit restart of the relevant history.

Historical information can also enter decision support through preference learning or consensus formation. Bayesian preference elicitation estimates a decision maker’s utility from comparisons, while minimum-adjustment consensus models consider the changes needed to reconcile multiple opinions [16], [17]. These problems differ from the present one. RSI-MCDM assumes that the current MCDM ordering is already available and does not infer a latent stakeholder preference. Its historical penalty is an explicit operational preference for continuity. That preference should be visible to users because it can change the order produced by current criterion evidence.

Historical information can enter a sequential decision system through time weighting, incremental updates, or a sliding window. A window gives recent observations a defined temporal support and limits the stored history. In RSI-MCDM, it supplies the monitoring signal; the optimizer separately uses the immediately preceding published order as its continuity reference.

The proposed rolling index is related to established distances between rankings. Spearman’s footrule measures aggregate positional displacement, and Kendall’s formulation measures pairwise ordering disagreement [18], [19]. Their distinction matters in a priority queue: a single alternative moving across many positions changes several pairwise relations, whereas two nearby alternatives exchanging positions may have a small aggregate displacement. RSI-MCDM uses footrule-type displacement for the gate and reports pair reversals separately. Entropy provides a diagnostic for how movement is distributed among alternatives, following the information-theoretic basis of Shannon’s measure [20]. None of these quantities is, by itself, a measure of maintenance utility.

sec.title: 2.3. Industrial streams and intelligent decision support
sec.p: Concept drift research establishes that a predictive model trained on historical data may become inappropriate when the generating process changes [21]. Recent work examines drift locality, feature screening, and adaptation in industrial streams [4], [5], [22]. Drift-adaptive anomaly detection has also been considered for marine sensor streams [23]. These studies justify treating temporal comparability as an engineering requirement. They do not justify interpreting a ranking stability index as a drift detector. The same rank displacement can result from sensor noise, a real process transition, an update to the predictive model, or a change in the alternatives being compared.

The relationship is particularly clear in predictive maintenance. Dynamic maintenance strategies use remaining-useful-life information, and cost-oriented evaluation of prognostic algorithms recognizes that prediction accuracy must eventually be connected to maintenance action [24], [25]. Explainable predictive-maintenance studies examine preprocessing, model complexity, and the interpretation of model outputs [26], [27], [28]. RSI-MCDM operates after these outputs have been transformed into comparable priority indicators. A raw failure-probability estimate and a cost estimate should not be merged solely because both are numbers. Their direction, scale, uncertainty, and operational meaning must first be defined.

Digital twins provide a possible host for repeated evaluation because they connect state estimation with prospective analysis. Recent contributions include manufacturing decision mechanisms, industrial robot decision frameworks, and synchronized logistics decisions [29], [30], [31]. Digital-twin development has also been discussed for apparel manufacturing and smart manufacturing more generally [32], [33]. A real-time machine twin and a simulation-based architecture for operational decision-making illustrate different levels at which such integration can occur [34], [35]. The temporal controller proposed here is a possible component of that architecture, but the simulation does not instantiate a connected factory twin.

A closer thematic connection is the integration of digital twins and multicriteria decision support for predictive maintenance [36]. Technology selection in logistics facilities similarly demonstrates the industrial relevance of multicriteria reliability and efficiency indicators [37]. These applications establish why an industrial priority layer is useful, while leaving open the particular problem of how a published ordering should react to repeated small updates. The present framework addresses that problem through an explicit continuity objective and an independently reported deviation from the current evaluator.

sec.title: 2.4. Scheduling research and the boundary of the contribution
sec.p: Dynamic scheduling research increasingly uses reinforcement learning to respond to disturbances, changing workloads, and equipment conditions. Recent reviews cover resilient manufacturing and dynamic job shops [38], [39]. More specific developments include additive-manufacturing scheduling, knowledge-graph-supported multi-agent scheduling, and collaborative robot task allocation [40], [41], [42]. Work on self-organizing production and scheduling with maintenance activities further demonstrates that priority decisions are embedded in constraints and feedback loops [43], [44]. These approaches optimize or learn operational policies. A temporal ranking layer has a narrower role and should not be evaluated as if it solved the complete scheduling problem.

For example, changing the ranking of two maintenance candidates does not imply that both can be serviced immediately. Crew qualifications, access restrictions, spare-parts availability, and production commitments may determine which action can actually start. Inserting RSI-MCDM into such a workflow therefore requires the rank output to remain separate from feasibility checks and execution authorization. The proposed alarm bypass concerns whether the temporal penalty is applied. It is not an authorization to execute an action and does not replace an independent protection function.

The research position is thus a temporal control mechanism for a complete priority ordering. Its novelty is the coherent combination of common-set monitoring, active-set anchoring, an exact squared-position solution, and an explicit bypass within a reproducible industrially motivated evaluation. The underlying MCDM methods, ranking distances, entropy, and sorting mathematics remain established components. The contribution does not depend on describing any of them as new, or on treating a lower reversal count as an unconditional improvement.

The controller then either retains the raw order or publishes the exact compromise between current positions and an active-set representation of the preceding published order.

sec.p: A related distinction concerns withdrawal. Removing an asset that previously occupied the first position shifts all remaining displayed ranks upward, but produces no reversal among them. The common-set definition has the same invariance for withdrawal as for entry. It does not erase an evaluator-induced reversal: if TOPSIS changes its relative ordering of two retained alternatives after a third is removed, the restricted comparison records that change. The construction therefore removes a bookkeeping artefact without claiming to eliminate the methodological rank-reversal phenomenon.

It preserves the previous relative order of retained alternatives while placing their historical targets inside the slots they collectively occupy in the current evaluation. A newcomer receives no manufactured past preference: both of its target terms equal its current raw position. A newcomer can still move in the final ordering because other alternatives compete for positions, but any such movement is measured by the current-ranking penalty. The anchoring step does not lock the newcomer to its raw slot.

sec.title: 4.1. Evaluation questions and controls
sec.p: The experiments examined four questions. The first was whether the temporal layer reduced pairwise reversals when noisy indicators were repeatedly evaluated. The second was whether that reduction coincided with closer agreement to a noiseless reference, rather than merely preserving an arbitrary old order. The third was how abrupt deterioration and candidate withdrawal affected the stability–response trade-off. The fourth was whether the implemented optimizer and the measured computational cost were consistent with the formal method. Each question required a separate observation; a smoother plotted trajectory could not answer all four.

The study used synthetic decision streams with known latent indicators and an explicit observation-noise process. Synthetic generation permits the same physical-state proxy to be evaluated with and without measurement noise. It also makes alternative entry and withdrawal reproducible. These advantages support controlled method comparison, while limiting the scope of inference. The generated records are not operating measurements from the authors’ affiliations, do not reproduce a particular production line, and do not establish industrial failure probabilities or maintenance savings.

Every configuration was evaluated with all four ranking adapters. For each adapter, the raw baseline was compared with RSI-MCDM and an unconditional-history control. The latter used the same anchor and historical weight at every epoch with a valid historical comparison, while retaining the same alarm bypass. Thus differences between RSI-MCDM and this control isolate the contribution of the rolling gate. A fourth control, fixed-bound TOPSIS, used the externally known indicator bounds without temporal stabilization. It isolates part of TOPSIS’s active-set dependence, but it does not isolate measurement noise from latent process variation.

Within each configuration, regime, and seed, all evaluators and policies received identical active identities and indicator arrays. The raw evaluator was identical between the baseline, gated, and unconditional-history policies. Policy comparisons consequently isolate changes in the temporal publication rule, with seed pairing retained in the uncertainty calculations.

sec.p: Membership affected evaluation and metrics differently. Each epoch’s evaluator used every active alternative. Consecutive-rank metrics used only common alternatives. A newly admitted alternative could therefore influence TOPSIS normalization, VIKOR regret reference values, or pairwise flows and thereby change retained alternatives’ relative order. The metrics recorded any resulting retained-pair reversal. They did not count the new alternative’s insertion as a reversal against a nonexistent previous position. This is the same distinction used in the mathematical definition.

The withdrawal-and-return regime introduced an additional membership intervention after full admission. Alternative 1 was removed for epochs 60–69 and returned at epoch 70. Its latent state and observation process continued to evolve during absence, but the evaluator did not receive its unavailable rows. On return, the temporal layer treated it as a newcomer because it was absent from the immediately preceding published order. This design tests active-set bookkeeping under a known interruption without assuming that an old rank is valid after an asset becomes eligible again.

The stream length is expressed in decision epochs, not seconds or minutes. A maintenance dashboard updated hourly and a production task queue updated every few minutes attach different physical meanings to the same five-ranking window. Converting the results to an operating schedule therefore requires a specified update interval and a decision about whether observations arrive synchronously. The experiment uses synchronous updates. Section 5.8 gives the S4 indicators a concrete maintenance-queue interpretation.

sec.title: 4.6. Noiseless reference and response measures
sec.p:
A reference ranking was generated at every epoch by applying the same adapter to the active latent matrix
Z t
, without observation noise. For fixed-bound TOPSIS, the reference also used fixed bounds. Top-choice disagreement is the proportion of epochs for which the published first alternative differs from the first alternative of that noiseless evaluator. The metric tests recovery of the adapter’s own latent preference under the controlled generator. It is not a supervised label of the best maintenance action and does not compare every method to a single universally correct MCDM ranking.

A second reference measure, composite-indicator regret, uses the mean of the latent priority-oriented indicators as a transparent shared utility proxy. At each epoch, regret is the maximum active mean indicator minus the mean indicator of the selected alternative. It is averaged across epochs. This proxy is useful for detecting a queue that is stable but routinely selects an alternative with lower aggregate latent urgency. Because the proxy is additive, it is not the native utility of VIKOR or the outranking adapters. Its limitations are stated alongside its definition, and no monetary interpretation is attached to it.

Recovery delay after epoch 45 is the number of epochs until the published top choice agrees with the current noiseless top choice for three consecutive epochs. If this run of agreement never occurs, delay is censored at the remaining horizon of 45 epochs. Agreement is checked against the reference at each epoch, rather than assuming that the shocked alternative is always the preferred candidate for every MCDM method. The reported average is the mean of these horizon-capped delays; the number of unrecovered runs is reported alongside comparisons affected by censoring. The metric measures reference recovery and persistence. It does not measure time to physical failure detection or intervention completion.

The noise regime has no imposed step, so its corresponding post-45 recovery statistic is only a background reference-agreement diagnostic. Primary response claims use the step and churn regimes. Defining this distinction avoids treating an arbitrary time origin as an event in the no-step stream. In particular, a long agreement delay in the noise regime can reflect ordinary uncertainty among near-equivalent top candidates.

sec.title: 4.7. Repetition, uncertainty, and implementation checks
sec.p:
Sequential evaluation requires careful separation of observation, prediction, and assessment, as discussed in stream-learning evaluation [49]. Each reported mean summarizes 30 independent seeded runs within its configuration and regime. Policies are paired by seed. Displayed uncertainty intervals are normal-approximation 95% intervals, calculated as the mean plus or minus 1.96 times the sample standard deviation divided by
30
. They quantify Monte Carlo variation under the stated generator, not uncertainty across industrial plants or distributions. When a policy difference is discussed as a paired difference, its interval is calculated from the 30 seedwise differences rather than by treating the two groups as unrelated samples.

The main comparison contained 360 generated streams and 4,680 evaluator–policy runs, corresponding to 421,200 decision epochs. The one-factor study contained 1,260 additional runs. These counts include the fixed-bound TOPSIS control and repeated reference settings within the sensitivity families. They should not be interpreted as thousands of independent industrial datasets. The independent replication unit is the seeded stream within a fixed configuration and regime, not every epoch and not every policy applied to the same stream.

The exact stabilization solution was checked by exhaustive enumeration for 72 random instances with two through seven alternatives. For each instance, the squared objective of the sorted-target output matched the minimum over all permutations to numerical tolerance. Boundary checks covered insertion without retained-order change, disjoint sets, the endpoints
ρ = 0
and
ρ = 1
, and the common-pair reversal count. These checks address mathematical implementation rather than empirical superiority. Passing them does not guarantee that the chosen continuity preference is appropriate for a particular operation.

Computational checks measured the evaluator plus anchor construction and exact stabilizer on six-criterion matrices with 20, 100, and 500 alternatives. Seven repeated calls were used at each size and method, and the median and observed maximum were recorded. Stream generation, metric calculation, file writing, and system integration were excluded. The environment used Python 3.12.14 and NumPy 2.3.5 on a Linux host. Timing results are descriptive for that shared execution environment.

sec.title: 5.1. Reversals under noisy repeated evaluation
sec.p: Table 3 reports the noise-regime comparisons for every matrix configuration and method. Figure 3 presents the corresponding opportunity-normalized reversal rates. Across the tested combinations, gated stabilization reduced pairwise movement relative to the raw evaluator. The use of the same streams within each comparison makes this a temporal-policy effect under the controlled generator. It does not establish that one MCDM method is inherently preferable to another, because their ordering semantics differ.

caption.title: Rank reversal rates before and after stabilization

sec.p: In S4, TOPSIS mean RRC decreased from 1,728.9 to 598.7, a 65.4% reduction based on the ratio of group means. VIKOR decreased from 2,594.9 to 897.8, and ELECTRE-net decreased from 2,023.9 to 672.5. PROMETHEE II decreased from 1,601.3 to 570.8, corresponding to 64.4%. These counts accumulate retained-pair reversals across the entire stream, including the admission phase. Their scale therefore differs from a count of epochs at which any reversal occurred.

The raw methods did not respond equally to the same indicator noise. VIKOR produced a higher reversal rate than TOPSIS and PROMETHEE II in the S4 noise regime. The thresholded ELECTRE-net output also differed from continuous-flow PROMETHEE II. These observations are implementation-specific and follow from different mechanisms: VIKOR uses normalized compromise measures, whereas ELECTRE-net assigns binary outranking edges and may generate tied net scores. They should not be generalized to every choice of VIKOR compromise parameter, preference thresholds, or ELECTRE ranking procedure.

Output stability increased alongside the reduction in reversals, but not every metric improved monotonically with more history. The reference-policy RD in the S4 noise regime was 0.0555 for TOPSIS and 0.0515 for PROMETHEE II. Thus the reduction required a measurable departure from the latest raw ordering. Expressed as average absolute positional movement per alternative, TOPSIS RD
×
19 corresponds to about 1.05 positions at a full 20-alternative epoch; the reported overall RD also averages smaller active sets during admission. This translation is illustrative and does not replace the exact normalized definition.

sec.title: 5.2. Agreement with the latent preference reference
sec.p: Top-choice disagreement in the S4 noise regime decreased from 0.258 to 0.182 for TOPSIS, from 0.299 to 0.242 for VIKOR, from 0.414 to 0.349 for ELECTRE-net, and from 0.228 to 0.152 for PROMETHEE II. These comparisons indicate that the lower reversal count was not achieved solely by freezing a preference unrelated to the latent evaluator. Under the slowly varying state and temporally correlated noise of this generator, historical ordering often contained useful information about the current latent ordering.

The improvement in reference agreement was not uniform across matrix sizes. In S1, VIKOR top-choice disagreement increased from 0.307 to 0.331 even though mean RRC decreased from 129.3 to 38.1. The smaller set and the compromise-index response therefore provide a case in which the reference temporal policy suppressed movement at a cost to latent top-choice recovery. This result limits any claim that the same historical weight improves decision fidelity across all adapters and set sizes.

The interpretation remains local to the reference definition. The noiseless comparator uses the same MCDM adapter as the noisy evaluation. It does not adjudicate between the adapters. For example, disagreement values for ELECTRE-net and TOPSIS refer to different latent top choices, and differences between those values reflect both noise sensitivity and each adapter’s score structure. Table 4 therefore presents policy comparisons within methods, rather than constructing an overall method ranking from a mixture of disagreement and reversal statistics.

caption.title: Comparison of ranking policies across stream regimes

sec.p: In Figure 4, the left panel compares reversal rates and top-choice disagreement across the raw, gated, and unconditional-history policies in the S4 noise regime. The right panel shows the percentage reduction in RRC achieved by RSI-MCDM relative to the raw baseline in the noise, step, and churn regimes. For the S4 noise regime, the gated points move toward both fewer reversals and lower disagreement relative to their raw counterparts. This pattern is consistent with noise suppression for the present generator. It would not justify a general assertion that smooth rankings are more accurate. The historical-weight sensitivity, discussed below, provides a direct counterexample in which a stronger continuity preference further reduces reversals but worsens reference agreement.

The composite-indicator regret measure in Table 4 adds a different perspective. It uses the same additive latent urgency proxy across methods, rather than each method’s own noiseless top choice. Its purpose is to expose an operationally interpretable loss proxy, while preserving the distinction between method-consistent reference recovery and shared additive urgency. A temporal policy can agree more closely with its latent adapter without being optimal for every alternative utility function. Neither result should be translated into a percentage reduction in downtime or maintenance cost.

caption.title: Ranking stability and reference agreement across control policies

sec.title: 5.3. Abrupt deterioration and membership interruption
sec.p: The imposed change at epoch 45 created a different requirement from suppressing repeated noise. Three indicators of the last asset changed persistently, and the first indicator could activate the observed alarm bypass. Figure 5 shows a representative TOPSIS trajectory for S4 with seed 100. The upper panel plots the raw RSI and its activation threshold, while the lower panel tracks asset 19 after admission. The vertical line marks the imposed condition change at epoch 45. The raw RSI remained a description of input movement, while the publication policy depended on both that signal and the alarm. The figure is an individual trace for interpretation; all performance conclusions use the replicated means.

caption.title: Ranking dynamics following an abrupt condition change

sec.p: In the S4 step regime, TOPSIS mean RRC decreased from 1,638.6 to 1,108.8, approximately 32.3%, compared with the larger reduction in the noise regime. PROMETHEE II decreased from 1,535.3 to 1,051.1, approximately 31.5%. This smaller reduction is expected because the alarm bypass frequently released the raw ranking after deterioration. Preserving a larger number of output reversals in this regime is not evidence that the temporal layer failed; it reflects the deliberate decision not to apply a historical penalty during an observed urgent condition.

TOPSIS horizon-capped reference recovery delay averaged 0.00 epochs for the raw baseline and 0.23 epochs for gated stabilization. PROMETHEE II averaged 1.70 and 2.30 epochs, respectively. VIKOR averaged 1.90 and 2.10, while ELECTRE-net had horizon-capped means of 6.80 and 5.60. For ELECTRE-net, 2 of 30 raw-baseline runs and 1 of 30 gated runs had no confirmed recovery within the remaining horizon. All S4 step-regime runs for the other three adapters recovered within the horizon. These method-specific values show that the bypass removes the temporal penalty when active but does not remove every source of reference disagreement. Noisy criteria, compromise normalization, binary outranking thresholds, and the occasional absence of an observed alarm can still influence recovery.

The withdrawal-and-return regime produced similar policy trade-offs. For S4 TOPSIS, mean RRC changed from 1,616.3 to 1,087.6; the corresponding values for PROMETHEE II were 1,515.0 and 1,031.8. Opportunity-normalized rates remained close to the step regime because the missing alternative affected a limited interval and retained-pair comparisons excluded its nonexistent transitions. This result supports the consistency of membership handling in the tested interruption. It does not establish robustness to extensive churn or to returning assets whose criterion definitions change during absence.

sec.title: 5.4. Contribution of the rolling gate
sec.p: The unconditional-history control is important because both controllers use the same exact stabilizer. Under S4 noise, its TOPSIS mean RRC was 581.8, compared with 598.7 for RSI-MCDM. Its top-choice disagreement was 0.183, compared with 0.182. For PROMETHEE II, unconditional history produced RRC 534.6 and disagreement 0.143, compared with 570.8 and 0.152 for the gated version. Thus the data do not show a uniform advantage of gating over unconditional smoothing at the reference settings.

The reason is visible in activation fractions. The TOPSIS gate applied stabilization in approximately 96.1% of all noise-regime epochs, while unconditional history applied it in 98.9%. PROMETHEE II activated in approximately 93.7% of epochs. A controller that activates nearly continuously has limited room to differ from its unconditional counterpart. The main demonstrated reduction at this threshold therefore comes from the historical-position objective, while the gate supplies an inspectable activation policy whose usefulness depends on calibration.

The fixed-bound TOPSIS control also clarifies the source of instability. Its S4 noise mean RRC was 1,640.4, below the vector-normalized baseline value of 1,728.9 but well above the gated value of 598.7. Removing active-set normalization did not remove reversals generated by repeated noisy observations. Conversely, this finding does not imply that temporal stabilization should always be preferred to external bounds: fixed bounds avoid some composition effects without introducing historical inertia, and the bounds themselves require a defensible criterion scale.

The observed gains are attributable primarily to historical-position regularization at the reference threshold. The rolling gate makes eligibility explicit and auditable, while the alarm bypass releases current evaluations during designated urgent conditions. The comparison with unconditional history defines the gate’s incremental contribution and prevents the smoothing effect from being attributed to the monitoring index alone.

sec.title: 5.5. Sensitivity to the historical weight and gate parameters
sec.p:
Table 5 reports the one-factor sensitivity results for S4 TOPSIS. Figure 6 visualizes their effects on reversal rate. Historical weight had the strongest qualitative effect on the trade-off. In the noise regime, increasing
ρ
from 0.2 to 0.6 decreased mean RRC from 1,588.7 to 598.7 and disagreement from 0.258 to 0.182. Increasing it further to 0.8 decreased RRC to 167.8 but increased disagreement to 0.273. The most stable tested output was therefore less faithful to the latent top preference than the moderate-history policy.

sec.title: 5.6. Alarm ablation and the price of apparent stability
sec.p: Table 6 summarizes the alarm-bypass comparison, while Figure 7 shows its effects on recovery delay and top-choice disagreement. In the S4 TOPSIS step regime, disabling the bypass reduced mean RRC from 1,108.8 to 591.8. However, horizon-capped mean reference recovery delay increased from 0.23 to 10.43 epochs, and top-choice disagreement increased from 0.098 to 0.209. A ranking evaluated only by reversal suppression would therefore favour the version that responded more slowly to the imposed deterioration.

sec.p: The ablation also clarifies what the bypass accomplishes. It does not improve the noisy raw score directly; instead, it removes an additional source of historical inertia during observed urgent conditions. The remaining difference from the raw recovery delay reflects epochs in which the noisy severity observation did not activate the alarm and the conditional stabilizer could still intervene. This behaviour is visible in the generator and implementation, so it can be investigated without attributing every delay to the MCDM method.

In the noise regime, enabling or disabling the bypass produced the same aggregate results for the tested seeds because no observation crossed the severity threshold. The unchanged outcome is useful evidence about this particular ablation, but it should not be generalized to a zero false-alarm probability. A different base-indicator distribution or larger noise innovation could activate the bypass without a latent deterioration. That case would require reporting unnecessary bypasses and their consequences, which are outside the present parameter experiment.

sec.title: 5.7. Computational checks
sec.p: All 72 exhaustive small-instance comparisons matched the objective minimum, and the boundary checks passed. These results establish that the implemented sorting procedure solves the stated squared-position objective on the tested cases. Together with the exchange proof, they remove the ambiguity between a permutation-level model and an unspecified optimizer. They do not validate the adequacy of the objective for a specific industrial cost function.

Table 7 and Figure 8 summarize the computational checks. At 500 alternatives and six criteria, median evaluator-plus-stabilizer times were approximately 0.95 ms for TOPSIS, 1.89 ms for VIKOR, 24.87 ms for ELECTRE-net, and 48.80 ms for PROMETHEE II on the execution host. sec.title: 5.8. Maintenance queue interpretation and decision audit
sec.p: A maintenance-queue example gives the generated indicators explicit operational meanings. The example uses the existing S4 step stream with seed 100, the same TOPSIS adapter, and the reference controller. Its twenty alternatives are simulated maintenance candidates M01–M20, corresponding to asset identifiers 0–19. They represent interventions competing for planning attention before resource-constrained dispatch. No new measurements or fitted performance values are introduced. Table 8 defines the six criterion meanings used in this interpretation.

Due-date pressure captures temporal urgency. Spare-parts readiness and access readiness describe whether the intervention can be prepared for dispatch. Their inclusion expresses a preference for actionable work among candidates already admitted as feasible. Hard exclusions, such as unavailable mandatory permits or incompatible crew qualifications, are checked before a candidate enters the queue. This separation prevents a high condition score from overriding a compulsory execution restriction through additive compensation.

The raw RSI was 0.9158, below the 0.94 threshold, so the historical penalty was active. At epoch 45, M20’s observed severity increased to 0.9623 and activated the bypass. Thus the example distinguishes continuity before escalation from immediate release of the current evaluator after an observed urgent condition.

The table is a decision audit rather than a measure of completed maintenance. It shows exactly which candidates would be presented first to the planning stage, and whether the temporal layer changed that presentation. A dispatcher would still apply crew, spare-part, permit, and production-window constraints before releasing work. Accordingly, the demonstrated outcome is queue behaviour: stable identifiers, valid entry handling, recorded deviations from current evaluation, and an inspectable response to an urgent indicator. Downtime and cost outcomes would require an execution model with observed or independently specified intervention consequences.

The example also clarifies the role of the alarm. Crossing 0.92 removes the historical penalty for the entire current ranking. It neither establishes a calibrated failure threshold nor guarantees that M20 is first under every possible MCDM method. A plant-specific escalation policy could instead impose a protected priority class before multicriteria ranking. That would be a different decision rule and should be evaluated separately. The present example retains the stated bypass so that every displayed ordering can be reproduced directly from the supplied stream and code.

sec.title: 6.1. What the stability improvement means
sec.p: The results support a specific mechanism. Noisy observations generate changes in current MCDM positions. When recent raw movement is sufficiently large, the temporal objective combines those positions with an embedded version of the preceding published order. Moderate history attenuates transient changes, and under a slowly varying latent state this can improve recovery of the current noiseless preference. The improvement does not require the index to identify whether each individual reversal was caused by noise. It depends instead on the information retained in recent ordering being useful on average under the stated process.

This interpretation explains both the favourable noise-regime results and the adverse high-history result. When the latent state evolves slowly, earlier order contains information. When a persistent change occurs or history receives excessive weight, the same memory can become a source of delay. The alarm ablation demonstrates the latter case directly. Accordingly, the framework should be described as controlled temporal regularization, rather than a detector that certifies which ranking changes are unnecessary.

The separation between input and output monitoring is essential to this interpretation. Input RSI answers how much the evaluator has moved in the recent window. Output transition stability answers how much the published queue has moved. RD answers how much the controller changed the current evaluator. Reference disagreement and regret ask whether the result is closer to defined latent comparators. Each quantity has a distinct denominator and unit of analysis. Combining them into a single undocumented overall score would conceal the trade-off that the method is intended to expose.

The scale of the index also matters. Normalization by $b$($b$ $-$ 1) is convenient and preserves bounded displacement, but its maximum possible value depends on the number of alternatives. A controller using a different normalization, such as division by the maximum attainable footrule, would need a correspondingly different threshold. The exact same numeric threshold cannot be transferred between those definitions. This is a mathematical comparability issue, rather than an empirical preference for one threshold range.

sec.title: 6.2. Industrial role and integration requirements
sec.p: For maintenance prioritization, the temporal layer could sit between a condition-based scoring service and a work-order planning interface. The scoring service would continue to produce current criteria and a raw ordering. RSI-MCDM would add a published ordering, an intervention flag, and an explanation of how much historical information affected the result. A planner could then inspect why a candidate with a slightly better current score remained below another candidate whose priority had persisted. The method’s value would depend on reducing avoidable queue churn without delaying decisions that are costly to defer.

The same principle can apply to production requests or resource queues when alternatives retain stable identities across updates. However, the objective is less suitable when executing an action changes the remaining system state immediately. In such a system, a static list may become obsolete as soon as the first task is dispatched. Integration would require recalculation after state-changing actions and a clear decision about which published order constitutes the historical reference. The current simulation updates observations synchronously and does not model action-induced feedback.

A decision log should preserve the raw score or preference-flow information even though the stabilizer consumes only ranks. Near ties and large preference margins are not distinguishable from positions alone. An operator reviewing a major positional change may need to know whether it reflects a small score difference or a substantial deterioration. Work on explaining MCDM results is relevant to this interface because explanations require preserving the intermediate evidence that generated an ordering [50]. The present model provides a transparent temporal component, but it does not supply a complete explanation of the upstream criterion evaluation.

The alarm bypass creates an additional integration point. Its criteria and thresholds must be chosen from the application’s intervention policy, not from whichever setting produces the most favourable RRC. A bypass tied to a validated protection or escalation rule could prevent temporal regularization from delaying an already identified urgent condition. A poorly chosen bypass could activate unnecessarily or fail to activate during a relevant change. The experiment demonstrates the effect of one observable threshold; it does not calibrate an industrial alarm or measure its diagnostic reliability.

An industrial evaluation would also need a definition of action cost. Reordering a dashboard display may be inexpensive, whereas cancelling a prepared maintenance intervention may consume labour and interrupt production. These are different operational losses. The squared-position objective treats movement through the queue as a generic continuity penalty. If actual changeover and delay costs are available, an application-specific objective might be more appropriate. Such a change would require a new optimization analysis because the exact sorting solution relies on the present separable squared-target structure.

sec.title: 6.3. Why the gate needs calibration
sec.p: A rolling gate is useful only if its activation region corresponds to a meaningful operating policy. At the reference setting, the gate activated on almost every noise-regime epoch, so it functioned mainly as a monitored route to historical smoothing. The experiment therefore provides no basis for claiming that gated control consistently dominates unconditional history. In an operating system, the gate might instead be calibrated using the distribution of accepted raw movement over a stable reference period, together with a defined tolerance for queue change. Such calibration would need separate data and evaluation.

The threshold response was steep in S4 TOPSIS. Increasing
θ
from 0.90 to 0.94 raised noise-regime activation from 26.0% to 96.1%. Threshold calibration therefore requires the input RSI distribution, the displacement normalization, and the applied alarm policy to be considered together.

Window length has a different meaning from the amount of temporal inertia. It affects the monitoring horizon but does not directly determine how far the optimizer moves the current raw order. Historical weight controls that movement. Conflating these roles can lead to a misleading explanation that a longer rolling window necessarily makes the controller trust old rankings more. In this formulation, the optimizer uses the previous published anchor, while the window controls eligibility. Longer windows can change how frequently that anchor is used, but they do not enter the squared objective itself.

sec.title: 6.4. Relation to other industrial intelligence methods
sec.p: The temporal layer complements upstream analytics and downstream optimization. Concept-drift adaptation can keep the indicator model current; MCDM can encode the decision criteria; RSI-MCDM can control publication continuity; and a scheduler can enforce feasibility. A favourable result in one component does not imply the reliability of the complete chain. A stable ranking of inaccurate health estimates remains problematic, and an accurate ranking can still be operationally infeasible if resources are unavailable.

This distinction is consistent with the industrial decision literature considered in Section 2. Digital-twin frameworks offer state synchronization and simulation capability, while reinforcement-learning scheduling approaches address sequential actions and feedback. The proposed controller neither creates a digital twin nor learns an optimal maintenance policy. Its industrial-intelligence contribution is a computationally explicit interface between frequently updated evaluation outputs and a persistent operational priority structure. It can be audited with raw input histories and does not require an opaque learned smoothing model.

The fixed-bound TOPSIS result further suggests that temporal and structural robustness should be considered together. Improving normalization can remove a cause of active-set sensitivity, but it does not make a noisy process static. Conversely, temporal regularization can reduce output movement while leaving the evaluator’s composition dependence unchanged. A deployment should diagnose both. If external criterion bounds are physically meaningful, they may be preferable to repeated sample-dependent rescaling; if the remaining raw output is noisy, a transparent continuity policy may still be useful.

The exact solution applies to the stated squared-position objective on complete permutations. Precedence constraints, protected rank intervals, or sequence-dependent execution costs would change the optimization problem. Such extensions require an assignment, mixed-integer, or scheduling formulation matched to those additional restrictions.

sec.title: 6.5. Limitations and transfer conditions
sec.p: The most important limitation is the synthetic evidence base. The generator provides reproducible latent states and noise, but it does not contain empirical sensor calibration, intervention records, or observed production losses. Independence between base criteria and the use of equal weights simplify a problem that can involve correlated degradation signals and conflicting stakeholder priorities. The findings therefore establish behaviour under controlled conditions, not general industrial effectiveness or a measured return on deployment.

The abrupt-change design is also limited. It imposes a persistent increase in three criteria of one alternative. Other relevant disturbances include transient spikes, multiple deteriorating assets, gradual degradation, contradictory indicators, and changes in the weight structure. A sustained first-criterion increase is particularly compatible with the chosen alarm bypass. The ablation establishes that this bypass matters in that setting, while leaving its performance under missed alarms and false alarms open to separate evaluation.

The noiseless evaluator is a useful reference but remains a model-based comparator. It assumes that the selected MCDM semantics and current criterion values define the desired ordering. Human decision makers may instead prioritize hard constraints, risk aversion, or cumulative workload. The additive regret proxy supplies one additional view, but neither comparator is an observed operational optimum. Validation should therefore include decisions and outcomes that are external to the controller, rather than relying solely on agreement with a ranking that shares its upstream method.

The experiments use complete synchronous observations. Missing values, delayed packets, out-of-order updates, changing criterion definitions, and uncertain alternative identity are not simulated. These conditions can make historical comparisons invalid even when the rank lists themselves are well formed. A deployment needs explicit preprocessing and versioning rules before the rolling index is interpreted. The supplied initialization and common-set policies address defined membership changes, not every form of data-quality failure.

The main factorial comparison remains small in alternative-set size. Runtime checks extend only to 500 alternatives and use seven repeated calls on a shared host. They do not characterize large-scale pairwise memory demands, distributed deployment, or bounded worst-case latency. The present implementation favours clarity and reproducibility. A production implementation may require more efficient data structures, blockwise preference calculations, persistent state management, and monitoring of execution delays.

Finally, the study does not establish a universal optimal parameter set or a general advantage over every temporal ranking method. Its controls isolate raw ranking, unconditional history, a fixed-bound evaluator, and the alarm bypass. More extensive comparisons could include score-level filters, uncertainty-aware ranking, and application-specific switching-cost policies. Such comparisons should use the same streams and independently meaningful response metrics. The present results already show why reversal reduction alone would be an insufficient basis for selecting among them.

sec.title: 7. Conclusions
sec.p: This study formulated and evaluated a rolling stability controller for dynamic multicriteria priority rankings in industrial decision streams. The method compares only alternatives shared by consecutive epochs, monitors raw ranking displacement over a sliding window, and conditionally solves a squared-position continuity objective. Historical positions are embedded into the current active set, and target sorting returns an exact valid permutation. An observed-indicator alarm bypass prevents the temporal layer from modifying the current evaluator during designated urgent conditions.

On paired synthetic streams with 30 random seeds, moderate historical regularization substantially reduced noise-driven ranking movement and improved top-choice agreement with the noiseless evaluator. In the 20-alternative configuration, TOPSIS mean RRC decreased from 1,728.9 to 598.7 and PROMETHEE II from 1,601.3 to 570.8. Their top-choice disagreement decreased from 0.258 to 0.182 and from 0.228 to 0.152, respectively. These results describe recovery of specified latent preferences under the controlled generator, rather than measured industrial cost or reliability improvements.

The controls established important boundaries. At the reference threshold, the gate activated frequently and produced outcomes close to unconditional smoothing. A larger historical weight could further suppress reversals while worsening reference agreement. In the abrupt-change ablation, removing the alarm bypass reduced apparent movement but increased TOPSIS horizon-capped recovery delay from 0.23 to 10.43 epochs. Stability therefore requires joint evaluation with current-ranking fidelity and response behaviour.

The framework offers an auditable temporal layer for repeated maintenance, production, and resource-priority evaluations. Its use in an operating industrial system requires application-specific criterion validation, alarm calibration, and evaluation against actual intervention outcomes. Future work should examine correlated and incomplete observations, joint parameter calibration on separate data, and action-dependent feedback. Those extensions should retain the distinction between raw evidence, controlled publication, and operational consequence that underlies the present method.
